extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, policymakers, and scholars interested in public opinion, propaganda, and the press
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and evaluative criteria for how public opinion and news/pseudo-environments are formed, shaped, and communicated — with emphasis on censorship, selection, and the psychological pictures people act upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictures in our heads / pseudo-environment
rubrics_metrics.description: What each man does is based not on direct and certain knowledge, but on pictures made by himself or given to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These interior representations (pseudo-environments) determine effort, feelings, hopes, and the direction of action. Examples: if a map says the world is flat or a dirt looks like gold, people act accordingly. Propaganda is an effort to alter these pictures to substitute one social pattern for another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions versus achievements distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The way in which the world is imagined determines at any particular moment what men will do; it does not determine what they will achieve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the difference between motives/intentions (shaped by images) and actual outcomes. Evaluation of behavior must separate the internal picture that produced the action from the objective results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship as a prerequisite for propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Without some form of censorship, propaganda in the strict sense of the word is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propaganda requires a barrier between the public and the event so that those who control access can decide what people shall see and at what. Military censorship is the simplest example, but other, subtler barriers (legal, social, economic) perform the same function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and wording of official reports shape perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities may present only certain facts and present them in ways designed to steady or direct public feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from wartime communiques: choosing moderate vs. alarming phrasing, omitting inconvenient facts (e.g., French ignorance of Douaumont) or inserting reassuring language; small word choices alter the mental picture readers form and thus their reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy norms determine what is withheld from the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of what constitutes a person's private affairs is elastic and determines the barriers to public access to facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different kinds of information (fortunes, salaries, directors' meetings, cabinet deliberations, treaties, health records) are treated with varying degrees of privacy; these conventions limit what evidence is available to form public opinion. Always ask how someone obtained the facts on which an opinion rests and who was permitted to see them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of correspondents and physical access
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations in authority control the selection of correspondents, their movements at the front, censor their messages, and operate the wires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical levers: selection of who may report, restricting movement, reading/censoring dispatches, control of cables, passports, mails, custom houses, and blockades. Such controls enable shaping of the news stream.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and formulaic reporting amplifies impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant repetition of phrases, statistical figures, and formulae in reports impresses audiences and helps create a persistent background image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: repeated casualty figures and recurring formulae ('mowed down by our artillery') created a striking effect that impressed neutrals and intensified a particular view of the battle. Repetition can substitute for argument and manufacture belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda constructs inferences by omission and emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: A mental inference can be produced not by explicit argument but by arranging emphasis and omission so a picture invites a particular conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: emphasizing German dead while omitting French losses produced an automatic inference that attrition favored the French. Evaluators must note what is left out as well as what is included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stored images, preconceptions and stereotypes direct interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages from outside are filtered by stored-up images, preconceptions, and prejudices which interpret and fill them out, and in turn powerfully direct attention and vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of public opinion must examine the internal filters (stereotypes, preconceptions) that identify and give meaning to fragments of information; these filters determine which messages are noticed and how they are understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of time, attention, vocabulary and speed reduce clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Public understanding is constrained by meager time available for public affairs, distortion from compressing events into very short messages, difficulty of making a small vocabulary express a complicated world, and speed of transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short messages and limited attention lead to simplification and stereotyping; evaluators should consider how compression and vocabulary limitations have likely distorted the event in public representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for independent expert organization to represent unseen facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative government cannot work successfully unless there is an independent, expert organization for making the unseen facts intelligible to decision-makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political science (or equivalent expert bodies) should formulate and present the unseen facts in advance of decisions, supplementing personal representation and preventing the untenable fiction that every citizen must form competent opinions about all public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: The press's economic basis causes it to reflect and intensify defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers necessarily and inevitably reflect, and therefore, in greater or lesser measure, intensify, the defective organization of public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers expect the press to overcome difficulties of public opinion at no cost; but economic and organizational pressures mean the press will mirror and amplify existing organizational defects unless public opinion itself is organized for the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on propaganda effectiveness from countervailing sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda control is never perfect because alternative and contrary sources (enemy communiques via wireless, soldiers' talk, leaks) can reach the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even powerful censors cannot fully prevent counter-information; naval/diplomatic censorship can be more complete than field armies, but wireless, neutral reporting, and soldiers' accounts erode total control. Evaluations should account for these countervailing informationsources.
